title: After Iran: A Scenario for Renewed Trump-Kim Summitry
gist: Contrary to conventional wisdom that Kim Jong-un has no appetite for more Trump summitry, a revisionist Kim could use renewed US and Japan summits to lock in de facto acceptance as a nuclear state while isolating South Korea, with China's stance now shaped by its desire to dilute Russia's growing influence over Pyongyang.

insights.claim: President Trump reportedly told South Korean President Lee Jae Myung at the June 2026 G7 meetings in France that he would restart diplomacy with North Korea, and later posted a photo on social media of himself strolling with Kim Jong-un at the Capella Hotel in Singapore.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Concrete, recent signal that renewed U.S.-North Korea summitry is actively being floated at the presidential level, a catalyst to watch for Korean-peninsula risk pricing.
insights.locator: U.S. President Donald Trump reportedly told South Korean President

insights.claim: During Trump's first term he met Kim three times in 2018-2019 in Singapore, Vietnam, and Panmunjom, producing one joint statement on peace and denuclearization, but the Hanoi summit ended with Trump walking out, leaving Kim embarrassed and deterred from further encounters.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Establishes the base-rate track record (three summits, one failed walkout, no durable deal) against which any renewed diplomacy should be judged.
insights.locator: During Trump's first term, he met with Kim three times

themes.theme: Why Kim might re-engage despite conventional wisdom

insights.claim: North Korea's pursuit of sanctions relief appears less of a motivation today because Russia has undermined the UN Security Council sanctions regime by vetoing renewal of UNSCR 1874, which established the Panel of Experts monitoring organ for sanctions compliance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Removal of the UN sanctions-monitoring mechanism materially weakens the West's main lever over North Korea, changing the calculus for what Pyongyang needs from any U.S. deal.
insights.locator: North Korea's pursuit of sanctions relief during the last round

insights.claim: North Korea has been supplying Russia with munitions, troops, missiles, and laborers for its war against Ukraine in exchange for billions of dollars in trade and military assistance from Vladimir Putin.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of North Korea's alternative revenue and support stream from Russia, reducing its economic dependence on any U.S.-brokered sanctions relief.
insights.locator: Any support from Moscow for UN sanctions has been replaced

insights.claim: At the June 2026 summit between Kim Jong-un and Xi Jinping, China committed to expand cooperation with North Korea across infrastructure, tourism, agriculture, and health.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Signals deepening China-North Korea economic ties running in parallel to Russia's, giving Kim multiple non-U.S. sources of external support.
insights.locator: China has also greatly ratcheted down compliance with sanctions

insights.claim: Conventional analysis assumes Kim has little to gain from more Trump summits, but this misses whether Pyongyang's foreign policy mindset is fundamentally revisionist rather than status-quo-oriented, as demonstrated when Kim opportunistically proposed a military partnership to Putin after emerging from Covid-19 isolation rather than simply refocusing on China trade.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Challenges the market/analyst consensus that Trump-Kim diplomacy is a dead end, suggesting investors should not fully discount the probability of renewed summitry.
insights.locator: What is missed in this conventional analysis

insights.claim: North Korea has concluded from the Iran nuclear deal experience that the United States now operates in a 'post-diplomacy' world where primary deliverables are grand but vaguely worded statements coupled with promises of follow-on negotiations, without real prospects of binding agreements, and that maintaining contact may be the best way to manage Trump's unpredictability and willingness to use force.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Frames the likely nature of any renewed U.S.-North Korea diplomacy as symbolic rather than substantive — important for calibrating how much weight to give any future summit headlines.
insights.locator: Pyongyang has learned from the Iran deal

insights.claim: A revisionist Kim would likely target a meeting with Trump after a U.S. midterm election loss for the party in power, avoiding detailed denuclearization talks and instead pushing for a peace treaty, an end to U.S. military exercises, and normalized relations — appealing to Trump's interest in a Nobel Peace Prize — to secure de facto acceptance as a nuclear weapons state.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Gives a specific timing marker (post-midterms) and negotiating agenda to watch for as leading indicators of a renewed summit.
insights.locator: If revisionist, Kim may target a meeting with Trump

insights.claim: If revisionism drives Pyongyang, Kim may also seek to reengage Japan, viewing Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi — a hawkish, politically maverick leader with strong public support — as a rare 'only Nixon can go to China' opportunity, unlike her mentor Shinzo Abe, whom North Koreans reportedly resented for turning hardline after initially supporting 2002 diplomacy with Kim Jong-il.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, named potential second front (Japan) for North Korean diplomacy alongside the U.S. track, relevant to Japan-Korea relations and yen-denominated regional risk.
insights.locator: The best chance for engagement is with someone of Takaichi's ilk

insights.claim: Japan has quietly moved away from its longstanding position requiring resolution of the abductions issue as a precondition for talks with North Korea, and Kim could seek a meeting with Takaichi to reaffirm the 2002 Pyongyang Declaration, potentially bringing billions of dollars into a normalization settlement.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A softened Japanese precondition and a multi-billion-dollar normalization settlement precedent (2002 Pyongyang Declaration) makes a Japan-North Korea opening more plausible than commonly assumed.
insights.locator: Japan has quietly moved away from its longstanding position

insights.claim: Pyongyang's broader goal is to achieve summits with both the United States and Japan as a nuclear weapons state — a feat no previous North Korean leader has accomplished — while dividing U.S.-Japan-South Korea trilateral cooperation and bypassing South Korea entirely, mirroring how South Korea isolated the North in the 1990s by establishing ties with Moscow and Beijing.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Frames the endgame as trilateral-alliance fragmentation, a strategic risk for U.S.-Japan-South Korea coordination that markets tracking Korean-peninsula stability should monitor.
insights.locator: Pyongyang's goal for such diplomacy is to achieve a position

insights.claim: Prior to Trump's first 2018 meeting with Kim, Xi Jinping held no meetings with Kim Jong-un, confident in China's influence, but once Trump's diplomacy started Xi met Kim five times to protect Chinese interests, then stopped meeting Kim from 2019 to 2025 after that diplomacy failed, only resuming after North Korea-Russia summitry began, including Xi's only overseas trip so far in 2026, to Pyongyang in June.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Establishes a clear behavioral pattern: China's engagement with North Korea reactively tracks U.S. and Russian engagement, useful for predicting Beijing's next moves.
insights.locator: Prior to Trump's first meeting with Kim in 2018

insights.claim: China could promote a renewal of Trump-Kim diplomacy largely to ingratiate itself with Trump while subtly diluting Russia's growing influence over North Korea, since Beijing is reportedly unsupportive of the trajectory of Moscow-Pyongyang cooperation but wary that direct intervention could sour relations with both.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Suggests China may become a quiet enabler rather than an opponent of renewed U.S.-North Korea talks — a counterintuitive dynamic worth tracking in Trump-Xi diplomatic readouts.
insights.locator: Given the current constellations of geopolitical forces

insights.claim: Should renewed Trump-Kim summitry occur under these dynamics, it would generate flashy headlines and a superficial reduction in tensions but would not address the fundamental issues of denuclearization or peace — which the author says may be the best that can be hoped for in a 'post-diplomacy' world.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Sets expectations that any renewed summit outcome should be read as symbolic, not a substantive de-escalation of the North Korean nuclear threat.
insights.quote: they would generate flashy news headlines and achieve a superficial reduction in tensions, but none would address the fundamental issues of denuclearization or peace
insights.locator: Should such geopolitical machinations come to fruition
